# What is shadow work?

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/guides/what-is-shadow-work

Manifestation · Decision guide
Shadow work — the practice of engaging the disowned parts of yourself — is one of the most-searched spiritual terms. The honest answer holds two things: the practice is a real, Jungian integration framework usable as deep self-reflection, and the supernatural “shadow clearing” claims aren’t supported. The practice can also surface material that needs clinical support. This page separates them.

Updated: September 2026 · Reading time: ~10 min · No signup, no email required

[Take the 2-minute pattern check](#pattern-check)
## Direct answer

Shadow work, in Jung’s framework, is the practice of engaging the “shadow” — the parts of yourself you’ve disowned, repressed, or denied (anger, neediness, ambition, vulnerability, and so on). The framework is real and usable: the practice involves recognizing these parts, understanding what they’re asking for, and integrating them rather than acting them out unconsciously. What the framework cannot honestly claim is to “clear” a supernatural shadow entity or to do energy work — the shadow is psychological, not energetic. And critically: shadow work can surface trauma material that needs clinical support, and the honest practice recognizes when therapy is the more appropriate response. The honest version uses shadow work as deep self-reflection without requiring it to be energy work, and with clinical support when the material warrants it. The two-minute Shadow Work Pattern Check on this page assesses where your self-examination is making real progress.

Your answers stay in your browser — nothing is stored, sent, or tied to you.

## Key takeaways

- **Shadow work is a real Jungian integration practice.** Engaging disowned parts of yourself through reflection is a genuine and useful framework.
- **The supernatural “shadow clearing” claims aren’t supported.** The shadow is psychological, not energetic; the practice is reflection, not energy work.
- **The practice can surface trauma material.** Shadow work can bring up content that needs clinical support — and recognizing when therapy is the honest response is part of responsible practice.
- **The honest practice is reflective integration.** Recognize the disowned part, understand what it’s asking for, integrate it consciously — not “clear” it energetically.
- **A reading can frame the reflection; it cannot clear a shadow entity.** Anyone claiming to “clear your shadow” is offering a projection — the honest version is perspective on the integration.

## What “what is shadow work” is actually asking

| You may be wondering | What you’re actually trying to determine |
| --- | --- |
| “What is the shadow?” | **Concept.** Jung’s framework — the disowned parts of the self. |
| “What is my shadow?” | **Shadow identification.** Which parts have you disowned — answerable through reflection. |
| “How do I do shadow work?” | **Method.** Answerable: reflective practices for recognizing and integrating. |
| “Can it clear my blocks?” | **Clearing attribution.** Whether shadow work clears energy — not supported; the mechanism is psychological. |
| “Is it safe?” | **Safety.** Shadow work can surface trauma — clinical support may be needed. |

The distinction that matters most: “what is shadow work” as an *integration-practice question* is fully answerable — the practice is real and useful. As an *energy-clearing question* it isn’t supported — and the difference is consequential, because the energy framing can extend seeking and delay clinical response.

## Why most shadow-work content is half-right in a way that misleads

- **It conflates integration with energy clearing.** The integration practice works; the energy-clearing claim doesn’t — and presenting both as one misleadingly grants the energy claim the integration’s validity.
- **It offers shadow-clearing services.** Practices to “clear your shadow” are framed as energy work — but the shadow is psychological, and the practice is reflection.
- **It skips the trauma-surfacing risk.** Shadow work can bring up trauma material that needs clinical support — and content that treats the practice as universally safe omits this.

## The honest practice, explained

- **Recognize the disowned part.** What have you repressed, denied, or disowned? Often it’s the qualities that were unacceptable in your family or culture (anger, neediness, ambition, vulnerability, sexuality, sensitivity).
- **Understand what it’s asking for.** Disowned parts often carry real needs — anger may be asking for boundary-setting; neediness may be asking for connection; ambition may be asking for direction. The shadow isn’t “bad”; it’s disowned, and it’s asking for integration.
- **Integrate rather than act out.** Integration means bringing the disowned part into conscious relationship — so it informs your choices rather than driving them unconsciously. Acting out (expressing the disowned part destructively) is not integration; suppression (continuing to deny it) is not integration either.
- **Recognize when clinical support is needed.** If the practice surfaces trauma material — childhood abuse, dissociation, persistent distress — a licensed therapist is the honest response. Shadow work is not a substitute for therapy; it can function alongside, and sometimes the clinical work is what’s actually needed.

## At a glance: what your practice looks like, and what it doesn’t settle

| You’re seeing | What it may indicate | Other explanations to consider | What it cannot prove |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A reflection that surfaced a disowned part | Genuine integration work — the practice prompted insight | The insight may come from the reflection, not the framework | That a shadow was “cleared” energetically |
| Strong emotion or trauma material surfacing | Trauma-surfacing — clinical support may be needed | The material may need a therapist, not shadow work alone | That shadow work alone is sufficient for trauma |
| Wanting the practice to “clear” you | Energy-clearing attribution — seeking a clearing | The shadow is psychological; the practice is reflection | That a shadow entity was cleared |
| Using shadow work to avoid therapy | Spiritual bypassing — avoiding clinical response | The clinical work may be what’s actually needed | That shadow work substitutes for therapy |

## What the research can — and can’t — tell you

- **The Jungian framework is a real tradition.** The shadow concept originates in Jung’s analytical psychology — a rich framework for understanding disowned parts and integration.
- **Self-reflection and integration are documented.** Research on self-reflection, emotional processing, and integration finds that engaging disowned parts through reflection supports psychological well-being — through documented mechanisms, not energy work.
- **Trauma-surfacing is real.** Depth-psychology practices can surface trauma material, and clinical support is the honest response when they do. The implication: shadow work is not universally safe; it’s safe when practiced with awareness of its limits, and with clinical support when needed.

- Zimmerman, M. (2017). *Shadow Work: A Complete Guide.* (On integration practice.)

## The five questions worth asking

### 1. Are you using the practice for integration or energy clearing?

Integration works; energy clearing isn’t supported. **What it suggests:** whether the use is honest.

### 2. Has the practice surfaced trauma material?

If so, clinical support may be needed. **What it suggests:** whether therapy is the honest response.

### 3. Are you using shadow work to avoid therapy?

Spiritual bypassing is a real risk. **What it suggests:** whether the practice is doing bypass work.

### 4. What is the disowned part asking for?

The shadow carries real needs — not “badness.” **What it suggests:** the integration the practice can support.

### 5. What would integration look like, honestly?

Bringing the disowned part into conscious relationship. **What it suggests:** the honest outcome of the practice.

**Why these five matter:** they separate the integration that works from the energy clearing that isn’t available, and they surface the trauma-surfacing and bypass risks. Answer them honestly, and shadow work becomes a reflective integration practice rather than a source of false clearing or bypass.

Common questions
## Shadow work — honestly asked

**What is shadow work?
**

Shadow work, in Jung’s framework, is the practice of engaging the “shadow” — the parts of yourself you’ve disowned, repressed, or denied (anger, neediness, ambition, vulnerability, etc.). The practice involves recognizing these parts, understanding what they’re asking for, and integrating them rather than acting them out unconsciously. The honest caveat: the practice is deep self-reflection, not energy work — the shadow is psychological, not energetic — and it can surface trauma material that needs clinical support.

**What is my shadow?
**

Your shadow is the parts of yourself you’ve disowned — often the qualities that were unacceptable in your family or culture (anger, neediness, ambition, vulnerability, sexuality, sensitivity). The honest identification is through reflection: what do you react against strongly in others (often a projection of your disowned part)? What qualities do you deny in yourself? The shadow isn’t “bad”; it’s disowned, and it carries real needs that integration addresses.

**Can shadow work clear my blocks?
**

Not through energy clearing — the clearing claim isn’t supported. The shadow is psychological, not energetic, and the practice is reflection, not clearing. What shadow work can do is support integration — bringing disowned parts into conscious relationship — through documented mechanisms (self-reflection, emotional processing). The “clearing your blocks” framing treats the practice as energy work, which it isn’t; the honest framing is integration reflection.

**Is shadow work safe?
**

Shadow work can surface trauma material — childhood abuse, dissociation, persistent distress — and when it does, clinical support is the honest response. The practice is not universally safe; it’s safe when practiced with awareness of its limits, and with clinical support when needed. If the practice surfaces heavy material, a licensed therapist is the appropriate response — shadow work can function alongside therapy, not instead of it. The bypass risk — using shadow work to avoid therapy — is real and worth noticing.

**Is the Shadow Work Pattern Check on this page personalized, or does everyone get the same result?
**

Personalized. You answer eight questions about your own situation — readiness to integrate disowned emotional traits, triggers in interpersonal relationships, and psychological integration versus spiritual bypassing — and your answers return one of five distinct patterns before the check suggests a grounded next step that fits yours. Two people can arrive with the same question and leave with two entirely different reads: it computes directly from your specific answers, not from a fixed signs list. It is free, needs no signup or email, and runs privately in your browser — your answers are never stored or sent.

**How do I do shadow work?
**

The honest practices: reflective journaling on what you’ve disowned (what do you react against in others? what do you deny in yourself?); identifying what the disowned part is asking for (anger may ask for boundaries; neediness may ask for connection); and integration — bringing the part into conscious relationship so it informs rather than drives. The practice is deep self-reflection, working through documented mechanisms (self-reflection, emotional processing), not energy work. If the practice surfaces trauma material, a licensed therapist is the honest response — shadow work alongside therapy, not instead of it.

How we approached this
## MysticDo’s editorial approach to “shadow work”

- **We separate integration from energy clearing.** The practice works as self-reflection; the clearing claim isn’t supported — and we say both.
- **We surface the trauma-surfacing risk.** Shadow work can bring up material that needs clinical support — and we say so plainly, because the bypass risk is real.
- **We explain the honest mechanism.** Self-reflection, emotional processing, integration — documented mechanisms, not energy work.
- **We do not clear shadow entities.** No reading, no quiz, and no framework on this page confirms a shadow clearing. The integration is what we inform.

# Which Chakra Is Blocked? How to Read Where the Friction Actually Sits

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/guides/which-chakra-is-blocked

Chakras & energy · Decision guide
Most guides answer this by handing you a list and a colour chart. The honest answer is narrower and more useful: a chakra is not a valve that jams, and almost nobody is fully blocked in every centre. What the question is really asking is **which energy centre is currently the site of the most friction** — the largest gap between what wants to move in your life and what is being stopped. Naming that specific point is the genuinely useful first step, and it is something you can read from the body and from where your life keeps sticking.

Updated: September 2026 · Reading time: ~12 min · No signup, no email required

[Take the 2-minute pattern check](#pattern-check)
## Direct answer

A chakra is not blocked the way a pipe is blocked. The seven-centre system is a **map for reflection** — a way of naming where in your life the flow has gone sticky — not a set of anatomical valves, and there is **no established way to diagnose** which one is “blocked.” What is real and worth working with is the friction itself: the place where something in you resists what wants to happen. Read it from **two signals at once** — a recurring theme in your life experience, and a persistent bodily correlate if there is one — and you will land on one or two centres rather than all seven. What no reading can do is diagnose a blockage; the goal is **balance** and range, never perfect openness.

Your answers stay in your browser — nothing is stored, sent, or tied to you.

## Key takeaways

- **“Blocked” is a metaphor, not a finding.** The seven-centre system is a reflective map. There is no scan, test, or reading that can establish that a chakra is blocked — so treat any answer that says otherwise as a claim, not a result.
- **Almost nobody is blocked — or open — in all seven.** The useful question is not “how open am I?” but “which centre is carrying the most friction right now?” Usually one or two, rarely more.
- **Read it from life, not from a list.** Life-experience signals are more reliable than body signals: look for the place where you consistently experience friction, not the difficulty that comes from outside circumstance.
- **Constrictions cluster.** Root + solar plexus + throat is the common anxiety-prone, high-achieving, voice-suppressed pattern; heart + throat follows loss or betrayal; root + sacral follows environments where emotional needs were treated as burdens.
- **The goal is balance, not maximum openness.** A perfectly open system would have no boundaries at all. Chakra work is about range — flowing enough to support each domain, and able to open or close as the moment requires.

## What the seven chakras actually govern

The chakra system is a South Asian contemplative map that describes the body’s subtle centres as a vertical series of wheels along the spine. Each centre is associated with a domain of experience — safety, desire, will, love, expression, insight, meaning — and the useful part of the framework is not the metaphysics but the *vocabulary*: it gives you precise words for kinds of stuckness that ordinary language blurs together. What follows is the most consistent cross-tradition account of each centre’s domain, described in flowing and constricted terms.

### Root — Mūlādhāra, at the base of the spine

**Domain:** physical safety, survival, belonging, groundedness, the body’s basic needs. **When flowing:** you feel secure in your physical existence, settled in your body, safe enough simply to be here. **When constricted:** chronic anxiety about survival, financial fear that outlasts the facts, feeling physically unsafe, a threat-mode that stays switched on even in objectively safe situations, difficulty being present in the body. The root is the foundation; everything above it depends on it, which is why chakra work almost always starts here.

### Sacral — Svādhiṣṭhāna, below the navel

**Domain:** creativity, pleasure, sexuality, emotional fluidity, the capacity to receive and flow. **When flowing:** you can feel pleasure without guilt, create without self-censoring, experience emotion as information rather than threat. **When constricted:** guilt around pleasure and desire, creative blocks, emotional rigidity or the opposite — flooding as the only available setting, difficulty receiving, numbness in areas that were once alive.

### Solar plexus — Maṇipūra, above the navel

**Domain:** personal power, will, self-esteem, autonomy, the capacity to take effective action. **When flowing:** you know your own worth without constant confirmation, decide from your own centre, assert yourself without aggression or collapse. **When constricted:** persistent self-doubt, chronic people-pleasing, difficulty making decisions, shame about your own worth, anxiety about taking up space.

### Heart — Anāhata, the centre of the chest

**Domain:** love, connection, compassion, grief, the capacity to give and receive in equal measure. **When flowing:** love moves in both directions — you give warmly and receive without deflecting, you grieve and open again. **When constricted:** difficulty receiving while giving generously, unprocessed grief become a wall, a fear of being hurt that has hardened into avoidance of real connection — or the reverse, compulsive merging because boundaries themselves feel threatening.

### Throat — Viśuddha, at the throat

**Domain:** authentic self-expression, speaking truth, listening, the alignment between inner experience and outer expression. **When flowing:** you can say what is true for you without excessive self-editing, you can be heard, your inner and outer life are reasonably aligned. **When constricted:** habitual silence about what matters most, saying what others want to hear, difficulty speaking in groups, the persistent sense that your voice does not matter or is not welcome.

### Third eye — Ājñā, between the eyebrows

**Domain:** intuition, pattern recognition, inner knowing, the capacity to see beneath the surface. **When flowing:** you trust your own perceptions, you can discern patterns that are not immediately obvious, you have access to your own knowing. **When constricted:** over-reliance on others’ judgement, an inability to trust your own impressions, confusion about what you actually perceive versus what you are told — or the reverse, an untethered intuition that produces anxiety rather than clarity.

### Crown — Sahasrāra, at the top of the head

**Domain:** connection to something larger than the self — call it consciousness, the divine, the universe, the collective. **When flowing:** a sense of belonging to something larger, a meaning that persists through difficulty, access to genuine openness and stillness. **When constricted:** feeling alone in the universe, an inability to experience meaning, spiritual disconnection — or the reverse, a spiritual bypass that uses transcendence to avoid the lower centres’ demands.

## How to tell which one is most constricted

The honest way to identify where the friction sits is to start with the body and with your life experience — *not* with a list you have decided to match yourself against.

**The body method.** Chakra constrictions often have physical correlates, which is part of why the map has lasted. Persistent throat tightness, chronic voice strain, or difficulty swallowing — throat. Chronic lower-back pain, digestive trouble in the lower abdomen, reproductive difficulty — sacral. Upper-chest tightness, chronic tension between the shoulder blades — heart. Recurring headaches or unexplained visual disturbance — third eye. These are not diagnoses. They are signals worth attending to, and worth investigating medically if they persist.

**The life-experience method.** More reliable for most people, and it is the one to lead with. Look at where in your life you consistently meet friction — not the difficulty that comes from external circumstance, but the difficulty that comes from something *inside you* resisting what wants to happen.

- **The root is constricted if:** safety is an ongoing preoccupation even when circumstances are objectively stable.
- **The sacral is constricted if:** creativity, pleasure, or emotional fluidity consistently feels unavailable or dangerous.
- **The solar plexus is constricted if:** your own will and authority are consistently subordinated to others’ expectations.
- **The heart is constricted if:** genuine intimacy — the kind that asks for vulnerability in both directions — consistently escapes you.
- **The throat is constricted if:** the most important things go unsaid, or your authentic expression is consistently unlike your performed one.
- **The third eye is constricted if:** you routinely override your own perceptions in favour of what you are told, or your perceptions produce more anxiety than clarity.
- **The crown is constricted if:** meaning and connection to something larger are persistently out of reach, and existence feels fundamentally isolated.

## The most common constrictions — and why they cluster

The system does not produce isolated blockages. Constrictions tend to cluster in ways that reflect developmental and cultural patterns, and recognising the cluster is often more useful than naming a single centre.

**Root + solar plexus + throat** is among the most common clusters in cultures that produce anxious, high-achieving, voice-suppressed adults. The safety system stays chronically activated (root), self-esteem is performatively constructed rather than inherent (solar plexus), and authentic expression is habitually traded for social acceptability (throat).

**Heart + throat** is common in people who have survived significant loss or betrayal and have protected against future vulnerability by closing both the giving-receiving centre and the authentic-expression centre. Love goes inward but rarely all the way out; the truth is edited to prevent exposure.

**Root + sacral** is common in people who grew up where emotional needs were treated as burdens. The body’s material needs for safety were met, but the emotional and creative life was implicitly discouraged — so the foundation holds while the fluid layer above it stays guarded.

## What chakra work actually involves

The goal of chakra work is **not** perfectly open chakras — a state that would leave you without any protective boundaries and permeable to everything. The goal is balance: each centre flowing enough to support its domain, with the ability to open wider and close down as each situation actually requires. What follows are practices associated with each centre; they are attention practices, not energy repair.

- **Root:** physical movement, genuine contact with the body, time in nature with bare feet on the ground, and treating actual physical needs — sleep, food, temperature, safety — as legitimate rather than secondary.
- **Sacral:** creative engagement without outcome pressure, permission to feel what is actually felt, play that is not optimised for productivity.
- **Solar plexus:** making small decisions from your own centre without polling; saying no to one thing a day you would otherwise say yes to out of obligation; naming what you actually want in low-stakes situations.
- **Heart:** allowing grief to complete rather than suppressing it before it finishes; receiving something offered — a compliment, help, affection — without deflecting.
- **Throat:** saying one true thing a day that usually goes unsaid; writing what cannot yet be spoken.
- **Third eye:** noticing your first impression of a situation before you edit it; trusting one perception a day without checking it against external validation.
- **Crown:** time in genuine stillness — not productivity, not consumption, just being.

## What the research can — and can’t — tell you

Two things are true at once, and an honest page has to hold both. The research literature says nothing about chakras as energy centres, and it is not silent on the *things people are actually doing* when they say a centre feels blocked.

- **What it cannot tell you.** There is no study that can locate a blocked chakra, because there is no accepted way to measure one. The modern seven-centre system with rainbow colours and quality lists is largely a 19th- and 20th-century Western synthesis, not an unbroken ancient doctrine — which is worth knowing before treating any version of it as settled fact.
- **What it can tell you.** The practice of turning attention to the body — which is what chakra work asks you to do — maps closely onto *interoception*: the sense of the physiological condition of the body. Craig (2009) linked the re-representation of interoception in the anterior insula to subjective feeling and awareness; Garfinkel and colleagues (2015) separated interoceptive *accuracy* (how well you detect internal signals) from interoceptive *awareness* (how well you know how good you are), showing they are genuinely different capacities. The relevance here is modest but real: a body-attention practice can strengthen the noticing that lets you detect where you actually hold tension — without any energy claim being true.

**Sources**

- Woodroffe, J. (as Arthur Avalon) (1919). *The Serpent Power: Being the Ṣaṭ-Cakra-Nirūpaṇa and Pādukā-Pañcaka*. London: Luzac & Co.
- Craig, A. D. (2009). How do you feel — now? The anterior insula and human awareness. *Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 10*(1), 59–70.
- Garfinkel, S. N., Seth, A. K., Barrett, A. B., Suzuki, K., & Critchley, H. D. (2015). Knowing your own heart: Distinguishing interoceptive accuracy from interoceptive awareness. *Biological Psychology, 104*, 65–74.

| Sacral | Creativity, pleasure, emotional fluidity | Creative blocks, rigidity, numbness | Your creative or emotional life feels unavailable |
| Solar plexus | Self-authority, confident action | People-pleasing, self-doubt, indecision | Your own will is consistently subordinated |
| Heart | Mutual connection, grief capacity | Walls, or compulsive merging | Intimacy consistently escapes or overwhelms |
| Throat | Expression aligned with inner truth | Habitual silence on what matters | The most important things go unsaid |

### What the signals can and can’t tell you

The signals people read as blockage, separated from what they can establish:

| You’re noticing | What it may indicate | Other explanations to consider | What it cannot prove |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Recurring throat issues when you go unheard | Friction in the expression domain | Muscle tension from held speech; a medical cause worth ruling out | That the throat centre is “blocked” |
| Chronic insecurity about money or home | Root-domain friction — safety and footing | Material instability, anxiety, or an overactive threat system | A root-centre diagnosis |
| A reader told you your heart chakra is closed | The reader’s framework speaking | No scan, test, or reading can establish a chakra’s state — the tradition’s own limit | Any chakra’s actual state |
| You can’t feel anything in meditation | Many possibilities — technique, readiness, nervous-system state | Expectation of specific sensations; the day’s state | That a specific centre is shut |
| Everything points to all seven being blocked | Usually one or two centres carrying friction | A symptom list read as total blockage is the framework misused as diagnosis | That all seven are blocked — almost nobody’s are |

## The four distinctions worth making

Instead of “which chakra is blocked,” hold four distinctions. Together they are MysticDo’s way of reading this question — a practical lens on what is actually at stake.

### 1. Reflection over diagnosis

A chakra blockage cannot be diagnosed, because there is nothing to measure. What you *can* do is use each centre as a prompt and answer from your own life. **What it suggests:** treating the framework as a set of questions rather than a set of results. **What it doesn’t prove:** that the felt friction is imaginary — the friction is real; only the label “blocked” is a metaphor.

### 2. Life signal over body signal

Body correlates are useful clues, but life experience is the more reliable read. The question is not “does my throat feel tight?” but “do the important things consistently go unsaid?” **What it suggests:** leading with the pattern in your life and using the body as a second vote. **What it doesn’t prove:** that body signals are meaningless — they are often the first place the friction shows up.

### 3. Balance over opening

The aim is not maximum openness. A system with no constriction at all would have no boundaries and would be permeable to everything. The aim is range: each centre able to flow, and able to close when the moment calls for it. **What it suggests:** judging progress by flexibility, not by how “open” you feel. **What it doesn’t prove:** that constriction is always good — chronic constriction narrows the range, and that is what the work addresses.

### 4. Care over clearing

When the friction is a health or emotional issue, the instrument for it is clinical or practical, not energy work. Clearing can sit alongside that care; it cannot stand in for it. **What it suggests:** routing anything clinical to a licensed professional first, and keeping the chakra lens inside its honest scope. **What it doesn’t prove:** that the lens has no value — it has value as reflection, and not as treatment.

## What is your chakra question actually about?

People arrive at “which chakra is blocked” with quite different questions, and which one it is changes what actually helps. The pattern check above can surface this for your situation; the currents below are the general map.

### What this pattern check looks at

- **Your starting point.** A feeling that something is stuck, a reader’s diagnosis, a health worry you have attached to a centre, or simply wanting to understand the map.
- **Four observable signals.** Whether you are reading the friction as reflection or as a literal blockage; whether the framework is standing in for a real response; whether your attention is on the body or on your life; and how much range you actually have across the centres.
- **Your actual question.** Whether it is the framework, the blockage, the method, or something the framework keeps pointing at — because that decides which next step fits.

Your answers classify one of five patterns — located friction, blockage-diagnosis, clearance-bypass, unlocated friction, or not enough evidence yet — then end on the next step that fits yours.

[Take the 2-minute pattern check →](#pattern-check)
## When self-inquiry runs out

Sometimes the framework does its part and the friction still will not name itself — and it is worth saying why. A throat-constricted person may under-report the throat constriction precisely because naming it requires the very expression the constriction suppresses. That is the legitimate case for an outside perspective here: not proof, but *a second read on where the pattern sits*.

A skilled energy reader or intuitive can often locate the most constricted centre with more precision than a self-assessment, because they are reading the field rather than asking you to assess the domain your own pattern is distorting. An [astrology session](https://mysticdo.com/astrology/) can contribute a chart-level angle too: in traditional interpretation, Saturn speaks to the root and to chronic constriction, Venus to the heart, Mercury to the throat, the Moon to the sacral — a planetary read of which domains tend to tighten for this specific person. Neither proves a blockage, and neither claims to. Each offers a structured mirror, which is the honest contribution.

## What you may actually be trying to know

“Which chakra is blocked?” usually resolves into one of five more specific questions — and which one it is changes what actually helps.

### 1. “Am I actually blocked?”

The diagnosis question, with an honest verdict: nothing can establish that. There is no test for a blocked chakra, and any reader, app, or quiz that claims to diagnose one is selling a result no tool possesses. The examinable version: ask instead “where in my life do I consistently meet friction?” — a question you can answer from evidence, and act on.

### 2. “Where would I even start?”

The entry question. Start with the root, almost always — safety and groundedness sit underneath everything, and work on the upper centres without a settled foundation tends to slide off. Then work upward only as far as the friction actually leads. The examinable version: spend two weeks on nothing but the base — sleep, movement, time on the ground — and see what loosens on its own.

### 3. “Why is nothing changing?”

The repair question. Chakra work is attention practice, not a repair procedure; nothing gets “cleared” in a session and stays cleared. What changes is what you do with the noticing. The examinable version: judge the work by whether your range in the constricted domain widened over a month — did you say one more true thing, receive one more gift without deflecting — not by how open you felt during the practice.

### 4. “Am I using this to avoid something?”

The bypass question, and the most important one on this page. Framing a real health or emotional issue as a blocked chakra can quietly become a way of deferring the response that would actually help. The examinable version: check whether the framework is producing more engagement with your life or an elaborate practice of avoidance. If a health concern is in the picture, the clinician comes first, not the clearing.

### 5. “What can a reading add?”

The reading question: a structured second perspective, not a diagnosis. An energy, astrology, or tarot reading can surface where the friction tends to sit and give it a workable shape. What it cannot do is confirm that a chakra is blocked — and the honest ones will not claim to. Frame it as “where does this pattern live?” rather than “which chakra is jammed?”

**Why this matters:** “which chakra is blocked” is one of the most searched questions in spiritual wellness, and one of the easiest to answer dishonestly — because a diagnosis sells better than a reflection. The honest version is narrower and more useful: there is no blocked chakra to detect, there is a place in your life where something in you resists what wants to move, and that place can be named from your life and your body. Read it as reflection rather than diagnosis, lead with life signals over body signals, aim for range rather than perfect openness, and let any real health or emotional concern go to care before it goes to clearing. The map is a good map. It is not a scan.

If you decide to book something
## Which practice fits your version of the question?

If you do choose a reading, match the practice to the form of the question — and here the useful frame is a second read on where the pattern sits, because the domain your own pattern distorts is the hardest one to self-assess. Different practices answer different angles of it.

| If your question is… | The honest fit | What it can — and can’t — do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| “Where does this friction actually sit?” | An energy reading, or an astrology session working Saturn and the chart’s tightest points | Can give the pattern a shape and a location; cannot establish that a centre is blocked |
| “Is my chakra blocked?” | No honest practice promises this | Nothing can diagnose a blockage; a session that claims to is selling certainty no tool has |
| “What should I do about it?” | A tarot reading, or an intuitive reading framed on the next step | Can surface a workable next action; cannot clear or repair anything |
| “Why do I keep going silent / giving myself away?” | A tarot reading working the pattern, or a therapist if it is clinical in scale | Can make the pattern visible and workable; cannot replace care if it impairs function |
| “Is this a health issue?” | A licensed clinician first — full stop | Nothing energy-related diagnoses or treats a condition; the framework can sit alongside care, never before it |

Before you book
## Before you book a chakra or energy reading

Two cases to handle before any booking. First, if what is surfacing is **clinical in scale** — a health symptom, persistent low mood, trauma, or a fear that impairs function — the instrument for that is a licensed clinician, not a chakra reading. A reading is a lens; it is not treatment, and treating it as treatment delays the care that fits.

Second, and specific to this question: **be wary of any reader who diagnoses a blockage.** There is no established way to diagnose one, so a reader who tells you that a specific chakra is blocked and needs clearing is offering you a result no one can verify — and a source that profits from the diagnosis being true is the least reliable source for it. A good reader will describe a pattern and its shape, not pronounce a verdict on your energy body.

And keep the frame honest going in: you are buying a second perspective on where the friction sits, not a repair. A reading that gives you a workable way to see the pattern has done its job. One that promises to clear a blocked chakra is promising something no tool can deliver.

## Frequently asked questions

**Which chakra is blocked — how do I actually tell?
**

You can’t tell in the diagnostic sense, because there is no test for a blocked chakra. What you can do is read where the friction sits, using two signals together: a recurring theme in your life experience, and a persistent bodily correlate if there is one. Lead with life experience — ask where you consistently meet friction that comes from inside you rather than from circumstance — and let the body be a second vote. Most people land on one or two centres rather than all seven, and that narrowing is the genuinely useful part.

**Is a blocked chakra a real physical condition?
**

No. There is no anatomical structure called a chakra, and no medical test can detect one as blocked or open. The seven-centre system is a reflective map from South Asian contemplative traditions — and the popular modern version, with rainbow colours and quality lists, is largely a 19th- and 20th-century Western synthesis rather than an unbroken ancient doctrine. The *feeling* of something being stuck is entirely real. The claim that it is a blocked energy centre is a metaphor, and metaphors are useful as long as they are not mistaken for findings.

**Can all my chakras be blocked at once?
**

Almost never, and assuming so is usually a sign of overload rather than insight. The system does not tend to produce blanket blockages; it produces clusters that reflect developmental and cultural patterns — root with solar plexus and throat, for instance, in anxious, high-achieving, voice-suppressed adults; heart with throat after loss or betrayal; root with sacral where emotional needs were treated as burdens. If everything feels blocked, the more honest read is that something global — exhaustion, depression, a life circumstance — is being projected onto all seven centres, and that is worth meeting directly.

**Should I see a reader to diagnose a blocked chakra?
**

Be careful. A skilled reader can offer a genuinely useful *second perspective* on where a pattern lives — particularly useful because the domain your own pattern distorts is the hardest one to self-assess. But there is no way for a reader to diagnose a blockage, and a reader who pronounces one is offering a result no one can verify. The distinction matters: “here is the pattern I see” is a reading; “your throat chakra is blocked and needs clearing” is a diagnosis dressed as insight — and the source of a diagnosis that profits from being true is the least reliable source for it.

**Does chakra work have any scientific backing?
**

Not for chakras as energy centres — there is no research that can support that, because there is nothing measurable to study. There is, however, real research on what chakra practice asks you to do: turn attention to the body. This maps closely onto *interoception*, the sense of the physiological condition of the body. Craig (2009) linked interoceptive re-representation in the anterior insula to subjective feeling and awareness, and Garfinkel and colleagues (2015) showed that interoceptive accuracy and interoceptive awareness are genuinely separate capacities. The relevance is modest but real: body-attention practice can strengthen the noticing that lets you detect where you hold tension — without any energy claim being true.

**What if the blockage turns out to be a health problem?
**

Then it is a health problem, and the instrument for it is clinical. A persistent symptom that you have framed as a blocked chakra — chronic digestive trouble, ongoing headaches, chest tightness, difficulty swallowing — deserves a medical investigation first and on its own terms. Chakra work can sit alongside care as reflection and relaxation; it cannot stand in for it. This is the single most important limit on this framework, because framing a physical issue as an energy blockage is exactly how the framework does real harm: it delays the response that actually helps.

**What is the goal of chakra work — fully open chakras?
**

No, and aiming for that would be a mistake. A system with no constriction at all would have no protective boundaries — it would be permeable to everything. The goal is balance and range: each centre flowing enough to support its domain, with the ability to open wider and close down as each situation requires. Chronic constriction narrows that range, which is what the work addresses; perfect openness would remove it entirely, which is not a state anyone should want. Judge progress by flexibility, not by how open you feel.

**Is the pattern check on this page personalized?
**

Personalized. You answer eight questions about how the friction is showing up for you — what brought you here, where you notice it in your life, how much range you have, whether the framework is standing in for a real response, and what you actually want to know — and your answers return one of five distinct patterns before the check suggests a next step that fits. Someone reading a literal blockage and someone using the centres as reflection leave with entirely different reads, because the check computes from your specific answers rather than a fixed script. It is free, needs no signup or email, and runs privately in your browser — your answers are never stored or sent.

How this guide was made
## MysticDo’s editorial approach to chakra questions

This guide is written to be useful to someone genuinely asking which chakra is blocked, which means it has to hold two facts at once: the framework is a rich and workable map, and almost every popular answer to this question overstates what the framework can do. Resolving in either direction would be easier and less honest.

Every claim here is either sourced or explicitly marked as belief. Where we describe what mainstream research supports, we cite it — and where it supports nothing about chakras as energy centres, we say that plainly. The history matters too: the modern seven-centre system with rainbow colours is largely a Western synthesis, and a guide that presents it as ancient fact is not being straight with you.

We do not sell chakra readings, we do not certify any reader, and we take no position on whether an energy body exists. What we do take a position on is the posture: treat the centres as prompts rather than results, lead with your life over your body, aim for range rather than perfect openness, and let anything clinical go to care before it goes to clearing. See [our methodology](https://mysticdo.com/methodology).

# Medium Readings

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/medium/

Category · Level 1–5 coverage
A medium reading is for **navigating loss and seeking connection or closure** — not for general life questions. The category deserves particular care: grief is real, vulnerability is high, and the difference between a responsible medium and a manipulative one is wide.

[Take the medium quiz →](https://mysticdo.com/quiz/medium) [Not sure? Do What Fits](https://mysticdo.com/do-what-fits)
[What it does](#what) [Psychic vs medium](#vs-psychic) [Who it's for](#who) [Questions to ask](#questions) [How to choose](#choose) [Providers](#providers)
What it does
## A medium reading, in one paragraph

A medium attempts to connect with someone who has died and convey messages or a sense of presence to the living person. Whether you treat this as literal or symbolic, the value people report is often less about “facts” and more about a felt sense of connection, meaning, or things-left-unsaid finally reaching expression.

### The short version

A medium reading fits when you are **navigating loss** and want connection or closure. It does not fit for general life questions (try psychic), reflective pattern-spotting (try tarot), or timing (try astrology).

The key distinction
## Psychic vs medium — the difference that matters

These are not the same service. A psychic reads your situation; a medium attempts to reach someone who has passed. Not all psychics are mediums, and not all mediums read current life situations well.

| Dimension | Psychic | Medium |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reads | Your current situation, people, decisions | Connection to someone who has passed |
| Best question | “What's going on with X right now?” | “Is there anything from [person] I haven't heard?” |
| Risk if misused | Wasted money on vague reads | Exploitation of grief; false hope |
| Vetting needed | Moderate — specialization, pricing | High — fraud risk is real, emotional stakes are high |
| Overlap | Some psychics are also mediums | Some mediums also do psychic work |

For the full comparison — including which questions fit which service and the grief-specific vetting rules — see [Psychic vs Medium](https://mysticdo.com/guides/psychic-vs-medium).

Who it's for
## It fits when…

- **You are navigating grief** and want a sense of connection, not necessarily facts.
- **There are things left unsaid** and you want a space for that, regardless of literal truth.
- **You're past the acute stage** and considering meaning-making, not crisis support.

### It does *not* fit when…

- You are in acute crisis — a medium is not a substitute for grief counseling or therapy.
- You want a guarantee of contact. No responsible medium guarantees a specific connection.
- You're seeking general life guidance — that's psychic, tarot, or astrology.

Questions to ask
## What to bring to a medium reading

### Approach the session with

- An open name or initial of the person — not a flood of biographical detail. Let the medium bring specifics, not you.
- One or two things left unsaid you'd want to express or hear acknowledged.
- Permission to yourself that the session may not produce the contact you hoped for — and that's not a verdict on the person you lost.
- A support person or follow-up plan, because readings can surface grief you didn't expect.

How to choose
## How to choose a medium — with extra care

Because the emotional stakes are high, the vetting bar is higher than for other categories.

1. **Look for evidence-based specifics** — a responsible medium offers verifiable details you didn't supply, not generic “I sense a father figure.”
1. **Watch for cold reading** — fishing questions (“does the letter M mean anything?”) that put words in your mouth.
1. **Refuse “curse” or “blockage” upsells** — the most common fraud pattern in this category.
1. **Read the refund policy before booking** — reputable mediums acknowledge sessions vary.

### Red flags

- Guaranteed contact with a specific person.
- “Energy clearing” or “curse removal” upsells attached to the session.
- Pressure to book longer or repeat sessions for “the connection to hold.”
- Refusal to let you bring a support person.

For the complete picture — session structure, costs, the evidence standard, and how to prepare — see [What Does a Medium Reading Actually Do?](https://mysticdo.com/guides/medium-reading-guide)

# Methodology & Trust

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/methodology

How we work
Spiritual services carry a real trust problem. We don't ask you to trust us. We show our work — where facts come from, how the quiz thinks, what AI does and doesn't do, how money flows, and where this site is still unfinished.

## At a glance
- **What we publish:** decision guides, comparisons, an intent quiz, and free tools — not horoscopes, not an encyclopedia, not a link farm.
- **Provider facts** come from the provider's own public pages, checked by us — never from reader-submitted bios or press releases.
- **Every claim has a class:** verified by us, platform-stated, user-reported, or editorial judgment. The difference is labeled, not blurred.
- **Affiliate links pay for the site.** They never decide rankings, and we say when free is enough — even when a paid option would earn us a commission.
- **AI is part of how this site is made.** What it doesn't do: decide conclusions, verify facts, or publish. A human does all three.
- **Honest current state.** Provider reviews are being written to the standard below and publish on a rolling basis; the quiz is rule-based. We'd rather say that plainly than let you discover it.

## The five questions

Before the details, the short answers to the five questions a methodology page exists to answer.

Who A small, independent project — not a company, an agency, or a content farm. Research and production are AI-assisted; a human reviews and approves everything before it publishes.

What The decision layer of spiritual services: which kind of guidance fits which situation, what things cost, how providers differ, and what to do next.

How Documented research: platform facts verified at the source, community signals read as patterns, structured editorial frameworks, and judgment that's labeled as judgment.

What we measure Fit (situation to service), price mechanics, transparency, safety patterns, and whether a service helps you ask a better question — not whether it's "true."

What we don't claim We don't claim any practice is real or fake, and nobody — including us — can guarantee a reading will help you. We help you decide what to do, not what to believe.

## Our position on spiritual services

MysticDo does not attempt to prove that any spiritual practice is "real" or "true." That question is outside our scope — and outside what someone deciding whether to spend $40 on a reading actually needs answered by us.

What we do take a position on:

- **If you decide to try a service**, we help you understand what it's for, who it suits, what it costs, and how to choose a provider.
- **We help you reduce unnecessary risk** — financial, emotional, and the risk of being manipulated by an industry that sometimes preys on people at their lowest.
- **We say when free is enough**, even when a paid option would earn us a commission.

## Who is behind MysticDo

MysticDo is a small, independent project. We are not a company, a media group, or a marketing agency, and we don't write as if we were. Research and production are AI-assisted — and a human reviews every page before it publishes.

This is also not our first site in this space. MysticDo grew out of an earlier, smaller psychic review project where the core of this model — decision-first content, documented methods, disclosed affiliate links — was tested against real visitors and real (small) revenue. That project is where we learned how expensive honest research is, and how much of this industry's "information" is marketing in a costume.

Two things carried over from that project: the method, and the lessons. One thing deliberately did not: **conclusions**. MysticDo's provider coverage starts from zero. When we reference industry patterns, we label the evidence level (see below). We don't inherit old verdicts — that would be exactly the kind of stale, unearned authority this page exists to prevent.

### How the work is divided

The pipeline is intentionally small and split into stages that cannot self-certify:

1. **Research stage** — gathering provider pricing pages, policy documents, and community-signal threads; assembling comparison data; drafting decision frameworks. AI-assisted for scale and consistency.
1. **Editorial review stage** — a human checks every material fact against its source, applies the evidence-level labels below, and decides what stays, what's downgraded, and what's cut. This stage cannot be skipped or automated.
1. **Publish stage** — only after editorial review signs off does a page go live. Pricing snapshots are dated at this step; corrections are logged in the changelog below.

The roles here are functional, not titular. We don't list individuals, because the trust model rests on the process — verifiable sources, labeled evidence, dated updates — not on a personality. When a real, externally verifiable identity is ready to stand behind specific pages, we'll say so plainly. Until then, the method is the byline.

## How we understand your intent

MysticDo is organized around what you're trying to decide, not around topics. We manage all content against a five-level intent model:

| Level | What the user is really asking | Example | Our investment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 — Curiosity | "What is this?" | what is tarot | Brief context only; we don't chase this traffic |
| 2 — Problem | "Can this help me?" | can tarot help with a breakup | Explain fit honestly, including when the answer is no |
| 3 — Comparison | "Which of these?" | tarot vs psychic | Full comparison tables with mandatory limitations |
| 4 — Purchase validation | "Is this worth paying for? Is it legit?" | are online psychics legit, psychic reading cost | Decision guides — our core work |
| 5 — Action | "Who do I book?" | best site for a medium reading | Provider recommendations under the standard below |

Our resources concentrate on Levels 3–5. That is a deliberate editorial choice: the curiosity layer is drowning in generic content, while the decision layer — where you're about to spend money and want someone honest in the room — is barely served.

### How the intent quiz works — and what it isn't

[Do What Fits](https://mysticdo.com/do-what-fits) and the four category quizzes ask about your situation, not your birth data. Under the hood, the current version is a transparent rule-based matcher: your answers map to a small set of intent profiles (love, life direction, spiritual growth, loss), and each profile maps to the guidance formats that structurally fit that kind of question.

The quiz uses psychological relevance — questions that recognize your situation — to make guidance feel personal. This is a deliberate design choice, and it has a hard boundary: **relevance is not diagnosis.** When a result says "people in your situation often benefit from a reflective format," that's a pattern statement about many people, not a claim about you specifically. If you're in acute grief or crisis, the quiz points you to professional support before it points you to any service — because that's the one situation where a wrong recommendation costs more than money.

Its honest limits: it's rule-based, the question set is small, and it doesn't learn yet. Quiz results are a starting point for reading the right guide — never a verdict.

## Three kinds of content, three methods

MysticDo publishes structurally different content types. Each has its own method, because each answers a different question. We never apply one method to another's job.

Decision guides
### Editorial framework

Built on the eight-step structure below. A guide earns its place by walking your actual decision — not by covering a keyword.

Comparisons
### Dimension tables

Fixed dimensions, a mandatory limitations row, never a single "winner." The decision stays yours — see the comparison rules below.

Provider reviews
### Provider standard

A fixed 13-part template with a mandatory limitations section and dated price snapshots. None published yet — placeholders until they're real.

A fourth type, **free tools**, exists for reflection and practice — the [Daily Card Pull](https://mysticdo.com/tools/daily-card) is a prompt for thinking, not a reading, and the page says so. Tools never upsell; they point to guides when a card isn't enough.

## How a decision guide is built

Every commercial guide follows the same spine, because the reader's decision follows the same spine:

1. **Problem** — name the actual situation you're in, in your language, not industry jargon.
1. **Context** — what this kind of problem usually is, and what it usually isn't.
1. **Options** — the realistic paths: psychic, tarot, astrology, medium, free tools, or nothing.
1. **Differences** — what each path actually delivers: output format, personalization, time scale.
1. **Risks** — the financial and emotional failure modes, including how this niche gets exploited.
1. **Decision criteria** — the factors that should drive your choice, stated before any recommendation.
1. **Recommendation path** — situations mapped to paths. Plural paths, because one size fits nobody.
1. **Action** — the concrete next step, even when the next step is "don't spend money yet."

A guide that can't survive this structure usually isn't a decision guide — it's a sermon or a sales page. If you find one of ours that reads like either, that's a bug and we want to hear about it.

## How comparisons stay honest

Comparison pages are where most sites quietly sell. Ours follow fixed rules:

- **Never a "best" verdict.** Fit depends on your situation — that's the entire premise of this site.
- **Fixed dimensions:** what question it fits, output format, personalization, time scale, typical price, who it suits, and limitations.
- **The limitations row is mandatory.** A comparison without limitations is an advertisement with a table in it.
- **The decision stays with you.** Our job is to make the differences visible, not to choose for you. See [Psychic vs Tarot](https://mysticdo.com/guides/psychic-vs-tarot) for the pattern in practice.

## How we research

Every material fact on this site traces to a source, and every source has an update policy:

| Information type | Source | Update policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider pricing | The provider's own public pricing pages | Verified at time of writing; flagged if more than 6 months old |
| Provider features | The provider's own public documentation | Reviewed each update cycle |
| Reader specializations | The reader's stated specialties on the platform | As listed; never editorially assigned by us |
| Review distribution | Platform review aggregates | Snapshot at time of writing |
| Community signals | Forums, Reddit, review sites | Read as patterns, never as proof; revisited when the pattern shifts |
| User scenarios | Composite and illustrative — never real users | Labeled as fictional on every page that uses them |
| Comparative analysis | MysticDo editorial, clearly labeled | Updated when the underlying material facts change |

One rule disciplines all of it: **we check the source rather than cite the middleman.** When a price, policy, or feature matters to a decision, it gets verified on the provider's own platform before it enters a page. When we can't verify something, we say so — and the claim gets downgraded to the evidence level it deserves.

## Evidence levels: what we know vs. what we think

Not all statements on this site carry the same weight. Every material claim belongs to one of four classes, and the wording on the page is built to show you which is which:

Level 1 — Verified by us We checked it on the provider's platform ourselves: listed prices, policy pages, available formats, reader directory behavior.

Sounds like: "Chat rates start at $X per minute, as listed on reader profiles."

Level 2 — Platform-stated The provider says so; we haven't stress-tested it. Useful, but it's their voice, not ours.

Sounds like: "The platform states it screens every applicant."

Level 3 — User-reported Aggregated from reviews, forums, and community threads. Genuine signals; individually unverifiable.

Sounds like: "Refund complaints recur across independent review threads."

Level 4 — Editorial judgment Our interpretation, framed as interpretation. It can be well-reasoned; it cannot be a fact.

Sounds like: "For your situation, a reflective format may fit better than a predictive one."

The rule that makes this useful: **numbers come from Levels 1–2, and anything worded as "may fit" is Level 4.** If you ever see a hard number presented as our judgment, or a judgment dressed up as a number, the page has failed its own standard.

## Provider reviews: the standard we hold

Provider reviews are where trust matters most in this niche — so they're also where we're slowest. Every provider review published on MysticDo must complete a fixed template:

1. **Overview** — what the service offers, factually and neutrally.
1. **Who it may suit** — matched to question types, never "everyone."
1. **How the experience works** — format, flow, and what actually happens.
1. **Pricing structure** — with the date the prices were checked.
1. **Types of readers** — what specializations actually exist.
1. **Strengths** — what the service genuinely does well.
1. **Limitations** — where it falls short. This section is mandatory; a review without it is an ad.
1. **Best use cases** — which situations it fits.
1. **What to know before buying** — the gotchas and the checks.
1. **How this review was researched** — the evidence levels used, stated on the page.
1. **Alternative providers** — because a review with no alternatives is a sales funnel.
1. **FAQ** — the questions people actually ask.
1. **Next step** — where to go from here, including "not this one."

Why a fixed template? To prevent the affiliate-review death spiral: *five stars → five stars → "click here."* A template forces the sections marketing would rather skip — limitations, alternatives, and the difference between what a platform claims and what users report.

### Current status, stated plainly

- **Zero provider reviews are published today.** Provider sections across MysticDo are placeholders, and they say so on the page.
- When the first real reviews go live, each will state when prices were checked, what we verified versus what the platform claims, and which community signals we weighed.
- We would rather have an empty shelf than a fake one. This is a choice, and it costs us money every week it lasts.

### Why you won't find overall scores here

You will not see a "9.4/10" next to any provider on MysticDo. This is deliberate, and it's the one place we diverge from most comparison sites by design:

- **A single score implies precision that doesn't exist** for subjective services. "Accuracy" isn't measurable across readers, sessions, or the person asking.
- **Scores hide the dimension that matters to you.** If you care most about price, a composite rating built mostly on other things will mislead you confidently.
- **Numbers invite verdict-shopping.** We'd rather you comparison-think your situation than comparison-shop our conclusions.

Instead, provider pages carry **structured dimensions** — pricing mechanics, transparency, reader vetting, formats, red-flag patterns — and you do the weighting. This costs us the simplicity of a league table. We think it buys you something better.

## Language rules: what we will and won't say

Trust is built or lost sentence by sentence. We keep two house lists, and every page is checked against them.

### We write

- "This type of reading is commonly used for…"
- "People often choose this when…"
- "If your main question is X, this format may fit better than Y."
- "This may help you explore…"

### We don't write

- "This will tell you your future."
- "Guaranteed accurate" — about any service, including our own guidance.
- "The #1 psychic site of 2026."
- Testimonial framing we can't verify — "she knew everything about me."

Two standing rules sit underneath both lists. First, **we never promise outcomes** — from any service, or from us. Second, **we never write as if a practice's truth were settled**, in either direction: devout belief and reflexive mockery are both positions you're entitled to hold, and neither is a job description for a decision guide.

## How we use AI — exactly where, and where it stops

MysticDo is upfront about this: AI is part of how this site gets made. We use it for research assistance — clustering community threads, surfacing recurring patterns, drafting comparison rows — and for production drafting. That's the honest sentence most sites in this niche won't write.

Here is the rest of the sentence. What AI does not do at MysticDo:

- **Decide conclusions.** Recommendations come from the frameworks on this page, applied by a person.
- **Verify facts.** Every price, policy, and claim gets checked by a human against the source before it stays on a page.
- **Publish.** Nothing goes live without human review — specifically on factual accuracy, affiliate compliance, provider claims, anything touching grief or crisis, and final sign-off.

If AI assists a page and we later find an error, that's *our* error, not the tool's. Accountability doesn't delegate.

## Affiliate disclosure & editorial independence

Some links on MysticDo are affiliate links. If you sign up for a service through one of them, we may earn a commission at no additional cost to you. This is currently the site's primary revenue model — we're not going to describe a fantasy version of this site where money isn't involved.

The more interesting question is what the money cannot buy:

- **Ranking.** Providers are not ranked by commission size. (We publish no overall rankings at all — see [why](#no-scores).)
- **Inclusion.** A provider is not recommended because it pays more. If it appears, it earned its place under the template.
- **Methodology.** The same template, the same evidence levels, and the same limitations requirement apply to affiliate and non-affiliate providers alike.
- **"Free is enough" calls.** When the right answer costs nothing, we say so — even when a paid affiliate option exists. You'll find this pattern throughout the [guides](https://mysticdo.com/guides/).

Two further commitments. If a provider stops offering affiliate terms, it stays on the site if it remains a legitimate option for users. If a provider changes its terms in ways that harm users, it is removed — regardless of what it pays.

And one structural rule about placement: **an affiliate link is the logical endpoint of a page, never its beginning.** The sequence is problem → judgment → comparison → match → *then* the link. If you ever find a MysticDo page whose reasoning exists to justify a button, that page is broken — tell us and it gets fixed or pulled.

## What we don't do

- Claim any spiritual practice is real or fake.
- Guarantee outcomes — theirs or ours.
- Publish overall provider scores. Dimensions, not verdicts.
- Sell rankings, placements, or links. (If that ever changes, sponsored content will be labeled in plain language, on the page, before you read it.)
- Publish fabricated testimonials or invented user stories.
- Present platform marketing as independent research.
- Treat user reviews as proof of anything except what users report.
- Recommend a paid service where free is genuinely enough.
- Replace licensed medical, legal, financial, or therapeutic advice — see the disclaimers on every relevant page.

One note on what absence means: **if a provider or reader isn't on this site, that's not a verdict.** It usually means we haven't researched it yet. We don't publish hit pieces, and we don't run a blacklist — we'd rather teach the pattern than shout the name, which is why our safety content focuses on red flags you can check yourself.

## Limitations

Intellectual honesty requires separating what will always limit this methodology from what merely limits it today.

### Structural — these don't go away

- **We evaluate services and decision-fit, not the truth of spiritual claims.** No methodology settles that question, and any site claiming otherwise is selling certainty it doesn't have.
- **Spiritual services are irreducibly subjective.** A reader who gives one person genuine clarity will do nothing for the next. No framework, including ours, can predict your experience — only improve your odds of choosing well.
- **Community signals are noisy.** Review platforms can be gamed, and forums over-represent extreme experiences. We weigh patterns, not anecdotes — and patterns can still be wrong.
- **Everything is a snapshot.** Prices, policies, and reader rosters change. There is always lag between a change and our verification of it.

### Current — on the record

- **Provider reviews are in progress.** None are published yet; the standard they must meet is above.
- **The quiz is rule-based**, not a trained model, and it doesn't learn from results yet.
- **Dating is real from September 2026 forward.** Earlier drafts carried illustrative dates; every page now shows an actual revision date.

These limitations aren't legal hedging. They're the honest boundaries of what a small, independent operation can credibly claim — and respecting them is what separates a methodology from a marketing page.

## How and when we update

A static guide becomes a misleading guide. Content in this niche has a short shelf life — prices move, policies change, readers come and go. Update commitments by content type:

| Content type | Cadence | Triggers an immediate update |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider pricing & offers | Rechecked on every page revision | Verified price change, new or expired promotion |
| Provider features & policies | Quarterly | Refund policy change, ownership change, verified safety issue |
| Decision guides | Every 6 months | Underlying facts change, error report, new service format |
| Comparisons | Every 6 months | New major provider, format shift (e.g., AI readings), pricing change |
| Quiz logic | When evidence says it's wrong | Consistent pattern of mismatched results |
| This page | Whenever methodology changes | Any change to evidence levels, language rules, AI policy, or disclosure |

From this page forward, revised pages carry real revision dates. A recommendation can move down or disappear — positions here are not sold, and not permanent.

# What we collect, and what we never do with it

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/privacy

Privacy
MysticDo runs on content, quizzes, and two analytics tools — not on your personal data. This page says plainly what leaves your browser, what stays in it, and how to change your mind about any of it.

## The short version

- Quiz answers never leave your browser.
- Two analytics tools (PostHog and Google Analytics 4) see pages and events — not identities.
- The only personal data we ever hold is an email address you gave us on purpose.
- We don't sell, rent, or trade data. There is nothing here to sell.

## What stays in your browser

The pattern checks and quizzes run entirely on your device. Your answers are saved to your browser's local storage so you can close the page and resume later — they are never uploaded to us or to anyone else. Clearing your browser's site data erases them completely.

The same storage holds a silent backup copy of email forms you started, so a failed submission isn't lost. It stays local under the same rules.

## What we measure

Like nearly every site, we measure traffic and usage — with two tools, chosen because both publish what they collect and let you opt out:

- **PostHog** (PostHog Inc., US cloud): page views, clicks and interactions, quiz events such as started or completed, device and browser type, and a rough location derived from IP (country or city level). No names, no email addresses, no quiz answer content.
- **Google Analytics 4** (Google LLC): page views and the same quiz events. GA4 sets the `_ga` cookies described below and assigns your browser a random client ID. GA4 does not log or store IP addresses.

What neither tool receives: your email address, the content of your quiz answers, or anything you type into the contact form.

## Cookies and local storage, plainly

| Storage | What it does | Lifetime |
| --- | --- | --- |
| _ga, _ga_* (Google Analytics 4) | Distinguishes visitors so repeat visits count once; remembers visit context | Up to 24 months |
| PostHog storage (cookie / local storage) | Keeps analytics sessions continuous across pages | About a year |
| MysticDo local storage | Quiz progress (to resume), and backup drafts of email forms | Until you clear site data |

Every mainstream browser lets you delete cookies and site data, browse in private mode, or install an extension that blocks analytics scripts outright. MysticDo works fully without any of this storage — blocking analytics costs you nothing except our ability to see which pages help.

## Email: the only personal data we hold

- **Subscribing** (the join page and email forms across the site) sends your address to **MailerLite**, the email delivery service we use. It is used to send exactly what you signed up for, and nothing else. Every message carries a working unsubscribe link.
- **The contact form** delivers your message and reply address to **contact@mysticdo.com** through Cloudflare's email routing. We reply from that address, and the correspondence stays in that mailbox.

We don't add anyone to a list they didn't ask for, and we don't share or swap email lists.

## Outbound partner links

When you click through to a reading platform or provider, you leave MysticDo — from that moment their privacy policy governs. We receive only an anonymous click event (which page, which link was clicked). We never receive your name, your email, or anything you do after the click.

## What we never do

- Sell, rent, or trade personal data.
- Run advertising or retargeting pixels.
- Build advertising profiles of visitors.
- Email you about anything you didn't opt into.
- Ask for sensitive information — there are no accounts and no payments on MysticDo.

## Your choices

- **Analytics:** block both tools with standard browser tools or extensions (for Google Analytics specifically, Google offers an official opt-out browser add-on). The site remains fully usable.
- **Email:** use the unsubscribe link in any message — or write to [contact@mysticdo.com](mailto:contact@mysticdo.com) and we will remove you.
- **Anything else:** if you want your email address deleted from our list and mailbox, say the word. We have no database of personal data beyond it, which makes that request easy to honor completely.

## Questions about this page

**Do my quiz answers leave my browser?
**

No. The quizzes run entirely in your browser and answers are stored locally so you can resume. Only anonymous events — that a quiz was started or completed, and which result pattern — reach our analytics. The answers themselves never leave your device.

**Can I use MysticDo without being measured at all?
**

Yes. Block analytics with browser tools or an extension, or browse in private mode with tracking blocked. Everything on the site — guides, comparisons, quizzes, tools — works without analytics running.

**Do you sell my data?
**

No. MysticDo's revenue model is disclosed affiliate recommendations when you choose to click through to a provider — not data. There is no data business here to sell into.

This policy describes the site as it works today. Material changes will be reflected here. Last updated: September 20, 2026.

Questions about any of this: [contact@mysticdo.com](mailto:contact@mysticdo.com) or the [contact form](https://mysticdo.com/contact). See also our [methodology](https://mysticdo.com/methodology) for how the site sources and discloses, and [about](https://mysticdo.com/about) for what MysticDo is.
